newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists pledge loyalty to Socialist govt.
newsitem.headline: French Communists pledge loyalty to Socialist govt.

text.p: French Communist leaders played down differences on Tuesday with their allies in the Socialist-led coalition government over policies on jobs and European monetary union, insisting they remained loyal.

"The Communists are an integral part of the majority. Our only ambition is to embody the profound desire for change that is present in our country," the Communists' parliamentary leader Alain Bocquet told Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin at a meeting at the National Assembly.
The Communists oppose French participation in a planned single European currency and have criticised the government for not moving faster to create jobs and boost the economy.
But party leaders sought to play down differences with the Socialists.
"We are totally determined to fight for the happiness of our people and the greatness of France. That is the reason for our commitment to the success of the left in power," Bocquet said.
His comments echoed statements by Communist Party leader Robert Hue who denied that party members' criticisms of Jospin signalled that the Communists might desert the coalition.
"Absolutely not," he said in a broadcast interview when asked whether the criticisms were intended as a warning.
"I consider the Communist Party today to be entirely within its role of a party which participates in the majority and in the government," Hue told France Inter radio.
The Communists' comments were meant as constructive suggestions, "to see what can be done right away to move forward".
In 1984 the Communists, citing policy differences, split with the Socialists and refused a role in later Socialist governments under President Francois Mitterrand.

Hue spoke a day after lunching with Jospin in the first meeting of the two men since a leftist alliance including Socialists, Communists and Greens won an upset parliamentary election victory five weeks ago.

After his talks with Jospin, Hue publicly urged the prime minister to take immediate action to combat France's 12.5 percent unemployment rather than put off decisions on key jobs programmes until the autumn.

Hue, who said he was not threatening the government, nevertheless reiterated Communist opposition to France joining European monetary union, saying the austerity required to meet the criteria for a transition to the euro would prevent the adoption of needed but costly social programmes.
Hue said there remained "a serious difference" between the Socialists and Communists over the euro.

Meeting the Maastricht treaty criteria for monetary union, which limit public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product, "would have serious consequences in terms of austerity and employment," he said.

Jospin ruled out more austerity during the campaign, vowing that jobs would be his top priority. But after taking office, he put off decisions until autumn on how to implement the potentially costly programmes he had promised.
He said keeping these promises would have to await results of an audit of public finances expected later this month.
